title: Sorting, binary search and invariants

objectives.text: Maintain a half-open lower-bound search invariant including duplicates, empty input and no-match insertion positions.
Choose a sorted-copy or in-place stable sort while preserving full record identity and explicit tie ordering.
Preserve the target candidate interval in a distinct rotated-sorted array without sorting it.
Return original zero-based indexes with logarithmic work per query and no duplicate-key guarantee.
Precompute exact weighted prefix cost for marginal rather than all-volume pricing.
Locate the active tier with a declared boundary convention and floor only once after summing.
Translate a lower-bound insertion boundary into repeated zero-based answers or -1 without re-sorting the ladder.
Merge closed intervals by sorted-start frontier, including touching, nested and zero-length windows.
Derive a sign-safe exact pairwise collision predicate over a bounded positive time horizon.

blocks.markdown: Binary search applies to a sequence sorted by the same ordering used by the search. It does not repair arbitrary input. This lesson uses prevalidated ascending Python integer lists and an integer target, with no mutation during the search. The task is lower_bound: return the first index i with values[i]>=target, or len(values) when there is no such index. This is an insertion position, not automatically proof of equality.

Maintain a half-open unresolved region [lo,hi). Every position before lo has value<target; every position at or after hi has value>=target. Start lo=0, hi=n, so both outside regions are empty. At mid, if value<target, discard positions through mid by setting lo=mid+1. Otherwise keep mid as a possible first answer by setting hi=mid. The unresolved size hi-lo strictly decreases. At termination lo=hi and the invariant gives the first valid insertion position. Never read values[n] without a bounds check.

blocks.source:
from bisect import bisect_left, bisect_right

def lower_bound(values, target):
    lo, hi = 0, len(values)
    while lo < hi:
        mid = lo + (hi - lo) // 2
        if values[mid] < target:
            lo = mid + 1
        else:
            hi = mid
    return lo

values = [1, 2, 2, 4]
position = lower_bound(values, 2)
print(position)
print(bisect_left(values, 2), bisect_right(values, 2))
print(lower_bound(values, 3))
print(lower_bound(values, 5))
print(lower_bound([], 2))
blocks.caption: Expected output: 1, then 1 3, then 3, then 4, then 0. For target 2, equal entries occupy indexes 1 and 2; left insertion is 1 and right insertion is 3. Target 3 is absent but has insertion position 3. The empty sequence returns 0, a valid insertion position with no matching element.

steps.text: Start [lo,hi)=[0,4). mid=2 and value 2 is not less than target 2, so hi=2.
Now [0,2). mid=1 and value 2 is not less than target, so hi=1.
Now [0,1). mid=0 and value 1 is less than target 2, so lo=1.
Now lo=hi=1. Index 1 is the first value>=2, and all earlier values are <2.

blocks.markdown: To test exact membership after lower_bound, require position<len(values) AND values[position]==target, in that short-circuit order. To count duplicates in a sorted list, bisect_right(values,target)-bisect_left(values,target) gives the equal-value range length. The library functions find insertion boundaries using ordering comparisons; do not mistake every returned position for a found equality.

For a random-access sorted sequence with unit-cost comparisons, the search makes logarithmically many comparisons by shrinking the interval. Sorting or validating the whole input on every query is additional work and can dominate that search. Inserting into the middle of a Python list shifts following elements, so bisect plus list insertion is still linear insertion work. A fast boundary search does not make every operation on a sorted list logarithmic.

blocks.markdown: A stable sort preserves the existing relative order of records with equal sort keys. It does not create a venue/event sequence that was never provided: if original order is undefined, stability alone is not a business tie policy. Declare any secondary key, such as (event_time,sequence), and whether it is trustworthy. Sort entire records or use one shared row permutation, never one column independently. The shallow new list from sorted still references the original mutable record objects.

Use a sorted copy when preserving the original sequence matters, and an in-place sort only when the caller contract permits that mutation. A dictionary can fit exact-key lookup under a unique-key contract, while sorted boundaries fit range queries. Evaluate the whole workload, preprocessing reuse, mutation cost, duplicates and memory rather than choosing binary search merely because log n looks small. This lesson uses the built-in stable sort; implementing merge sort or quicksort needs its own algorithm teaching.

Independent transfer: implement lower_bound from the invariant before viewing the code, then compare with bisect_left on generated sorted integer fixtures. Include empty/all-equal, target below/above every value, absent interior target and duplicate runs. Add a membership wrapper with the bounds-first check. Then sort equal-key records by a declared secondary key and verify stable order and caller-mutation policy separately.

References: [bisect](https://docs.python.org/3/library/bisect.html) for insertion boundaries and search-versus-insertion costs; [Python sorting](https://docs.python.org/3/howto/sorting.html) for sorted/list.sort and stability. Fixtures and ordering contracts are synthetic. No C++ toolchain or production feed ordering is certified by this Python example.

A different search precondition

Ordinary lower_bound needs global sortedness; a rotated ladder is not globally sorted. Public input: 1..200000 distinct integers of absolute value<=1e9, rotated from increasing order; 1..200000 queries. Return one STRING line per query, containing its original zero-based index or -1. Sorting the ladder would destroy these indexes. We trust the guaranteed precondition, rather than doing a full linear validation inside every query.

Candidate invariant and sorted half

Use inclusive [lo,hi]. If a[mid] equals the target, return mid. Otherwise at least one of [lo,mid] and [mid,hi] is increasing: a distinct rotated interval contains at most one descent. If a[lo]<=a[mid], the left side is sorted. The target belongs there exactly when a[lo]<=target<a[mid]; keep hi=mid-1 then, otherwise keep lo=mid+1. If left is not sorted, right is sorted: keep lo=mid+1 only when a[mid]<target<=a[hi], otherwise hi=mid-1. Every discarded half is proved unable to hold a still-missing target.

Proof, trace and boundaries

Initially every possible index is in [0,n-1]. Each test preserves the invariant: if present and not yet returned, target lies in [lo,hi]. Each update excludes the already-tested mid and strictly shrinks the candidate interval by about half. Empty interval proves absence. In [4,5,6,7,0,1,2], target0: mid3 has7,left sorted but0 outside[4,7); keep[4,6]. mid5 has1,left[0,1] sorted and0 inside; keep[4,4],return4. Target4 must retain the left endpoint through <=. Singletons, unrotated arrays and negative targets use the same logic.

Scope, cost and transfer

O(log n) comparisons per query, O(q log n) total and O(q) returned lines; algorithmic working space per query is O(1). Do not claim logarithmic worst case if duplicate keys are allowed: equal endpoints can hide the pivot. Exhaustively rotate tiny increasing arrays, compare every present/absent query to linear lookup, and exercise n=q=200000 separately. Preserve original input and query order; repeated queries repeat their answer.

blocks.caption: Expected ['4', '-1', '0', '6'], then ['0', '-1']. Distinct rotated input is a source guarantee, not checked once per lookup.

Marginal pricing and rate units

The task has 1 to 50 tiers, increasing positive boundaries at most 10^12, rates from 0 to 10,000, and up to 90,000 query volumes from 0 to 10^12. Tier j covers (a[j-1], a[j]], with the final upper bound infinite.

Rates are hundredths of a basis point: 100 means 1 bp; 10000 means 100 bp, or 1 percent. The fee is floor(sum(rate*part)/1000000). Each volume slice gets its own rate. Applying the final tier's rate to all volume is a different pricing rule. build(bounds, rates) runs once; fee(model, volume) returns an integer.

Keep an exact prefix numerator

Set P[0]=0. For each finite tier j, set P[j+1]=P[j]+(bounds[j]-lower)*rates[j], where lower is zero or the previous boundary. P[k] is the exact unrounded numerator for every tier before k.

Store boundaries, rates, and prefixes together as immutable tuples. Never floor each tier separately: discarded fractions can combine into a whole unit. Add exact numerators first and divide once by 1000000.

Boundary search proof

k=bisect_left(bounds, V) finds the first finite boundary at least V, or len(bounds) for the final tier. All preceding finite tiers are full. The active width is V minus zero when k=0, otherwise V-bounds[k-1]. Add width*rates[k] to P[k].

At an exact boundary, left search uses the preceding tier at its full width. Right search could also work with the next tier at zero width and the matching prefix, but mixing these index conventions breaks the formula. V=0 and an empty boundary list both work. Sorted boundaries are a source guarantee; never sort them independently of their rates.

Trace, one-floor counterexample, and bounds

For boundaries [1000000,5000000], rates [10000,8000,5000], and V=7000000, the weighted numerator is 10000*1000000 + 8000*4000000 + 5000*2000000 = 52000000000. Divide by 1000000 to get 52000. Applying the last rate to all volume would wrongly give 35000.

Two tier contributions with numerator 600000 each sum to 1200000: flooring the total gives 1, but flooring each gives 0. Total numerator is at most 10^16 because disjoint tier widths sum to V; it is not 50 times that bound. Use promoted 64-bit multiplication in a fixed-width language.

Cost and independent transfer

Build takes O(t), each query O(log t), model storage O(t), and returned output O(q). A separate oracle loops over all tiers, clips each overlap with [0,V], sums exact products, then floors once.

Test boundaries and their neighbors, zero, the final unbounded tier, one tier, zero rates, nonmonotone rates, 50 tiers and 90,000 queries. Rates need not decrease. This is an algorithm for a supplied synthetic schedule, not a claim about current exchange prices or a payment action.

blocks.source:
MOD = 1000000007

def build(bounds, rates):
    cumulative = [0]
    previous = 0
    for (bound, rate) in zip(bounds, rates):
        cumulative.append(cumulative[-1] + (bound - previous) * rate)
        previous = bound
    return (tuple(bounds), tuple(rates), tuple(cumulative))

def fee(model, volume):
    from bisect import bisect_left
    (bounds, rates, cumulative) = model
    tier = bisect_left(bounds, volume)
    lower = 0 if tier == 0 else bounds[tier - 1]
    numerator = cumulative[tier] + (volume - lower) * rates[tier]
    return numerator // 1000000

model = build([1000000, 5000000], [10000, 8000, 5000])
print([fee(model, v) for v in [500000, 1000000, 7000000]])
print(fee(build([], [10000]), 0))

Reuse the proven boundary

The existing lower_bound returns an insertion position in 0..n. The practice task wants that position only when it is less than n; otherwise output -1. It does not require equality with the query: the first larger price qualifies too. The sorted array is immutable, duplicates are allowed, and each query starts a fresh lo=0, hi=n search.

Trace the sentinel rather than indexing it

For [2,4,4,7], queries 4,5,8 give positions 1,3,4 and output lines 1,3,-1. Position 4 is not an array element. A query below all prices yields 0. Do not use bisect_right, which skips equal prices, or a membership wrapper, which rejects a larger qualifying rung.

Cost and transfer

Each interval shrinks geometrically: O(log n) comparisons per query, O(m log n) total, and O(m) returned output storage. n,m may each reach 200000. The function returns strings because the supplied main prints each returned line. Compare against a linear first-qualifying scan on small fixtures, then test the largest equal-value ladder. No sorting or per-query copying is needed.

Closed union, not half-open scheduling

These halt windows are closed [s,e], with s<=e. Two windows sharing an endpoint overlap, so [1,4] and [4,6] merge. [1,4] and [5,6] do not overlap and remain separate, despite adjacent integer labels. This differs from the half-open interval-selection problem, where an event starting at the previous end is compatible.

Sorted frontier invariant and proof

Process a sorted COPY of (start,end) pairs by increasing start. The output is a sorted sequence of disjoint merged windows representing exactly the processed union. If the next start exceeds the last merged end, it cannot overlap any earlier window, so append it. Otherwise extend only the last end to max(old_end,next_end). Using next_end directly would incorrectly shrink a containing interval. No earlier output can be affected because its end is strictly before the current frontier start.

Trace, mutation and cost

[(4,6),(1,4),(2,3),(8,8)] sorts to [(1,4),(2,3),(4,6),(8,8)] and becomes [(1,6),(8,8)]. Identical/nested intervals add no coverage, while a singleton [8,8] is legal. The helper creates fresh mutable pairs rather than changing caller rows. With n<=100000, sorting costs O(n log n), the scan O(n), and result/copy storage O(n). Test permutation invariance and compare covered closed endpoints/segments on small fixtures.

Solve the meeting equation before dividing

Agents i,j meet when x_i+v_i*tau=x_j+v_j*tau. Define distance=x_i-x_j and closing=v_j-v_i, so tau=distance/closing. Distinct starting positions exclude tau=0. A strictly positive meeting time requires distance and closing to have the same nonzero sign. Then tau<=t is exactly abs(distance)<=t*abs(closing). Equal velocities cannot collide from distinct positions.

Exact cross products preserve endpoint semantics

The implementation tests distance*closing>0 and the cross-multiplied horizon bound, without floating division. Equality at tau=t counts; a meeting after t or in the past does not. For x=[0,10],v=[3,1], meeting time 5 counts at horizon 5 but not 4. Initial input order is arbitrary; the signed predicate works in either index order. Sorting is not required for the stated pairwise design.

Bounds and transfer

n<=2000 allows O(n^2) pair checks. Coordinate/velocity differences have magnitude<=2*10^9, and t<=10^9, so products used here remain within signed 64-bit range; Python integers are exact. Do not interpret a general claim about double precision as exact representation of every large integer. Test equal velocities, separating motion, negative coordinates, opposite directions and equality at the horizon against exact rational meeting times. This is a synthetic trajectory calculation, not a collision safety system.

blocks.source:
from collections import OrderedDict, deque
from bisect import bisect_left
import heapq
import math

def collision_risk(x, v, t):
    for i in range(len(x)):
        for j in range(i):
            distance = x[i] - x[j]
            closing = v[j] - v[i]
            if distance * closing > 0 and abs(distance) <= t * abs(closing):
                return ['COLLIDE']
    return ['SAFE']

print(*collision_risk([0, 10], [3, 1], 5))
print(*collision_risk([0, 10], [3, 1], 4))
